_meta.note: Standard 3.1 renamed 'Digital Citizenship Advocate' in v4.02.

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders ensure all students learn from educators who are skilled in using technology to create authentic and engaging learning experiences.
met_criteria: Has a clear picture of educator technology competency across the school
Invests in sustained, differentiated development to build technology-for-learning skills
Evaluates educator practice in this area as part of professional review
Ensures technology competency development is tied to student learning impact, not just tool proficiency
not_yet_met_criteria: Technology CPD is offered but not monitored for impact on classroom practice
Does not review educator technology competency systematically
Technology skills development is treated as optional professional development
partial_indicators: Ensures all educators have access to technology CPD but does not monitor uptake, quality of practice, or impact on student learning experiences

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders ensure access to technology, connectivity, inclusive digital content and learning environments that meet the needs of all students.
met_criteria: Has a complete picture of access inequities affecting students in their institution
Takes active steps to close identified access gaps — not just document them
Ensures digital content and environments are inclusive, not just accessible
Access equity is a leadership priority, not an infrastructure footnote
not_yet_met_criteria: Assumes students have equivalent access to technology and connectivity
Does not systematically audit or address access inequities
partial_indicators: Provides device loan schemes and print alternatives for students without home access but does not audit whether digital content and environments are genuinely inclusive for students with diverse learning needs

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders model the use of technology in inclusive, healthy ways to solve problems and strengthen community.
met_criteria: Is visibly and deliberately using technology to solve institutional problems and communicate with community
Demonstrates healthy technology practices in their own leadership behaviour (e.g., email boundaries, meeting culture)
Uses technology to strengthen — not replace — human community connections
Models the inclusive use of technology in how they communicate and engage
not_yet_met_criteria: Technology use in their own leadership is unreflective and not modelled deliberately
Does not consider what their technology behaviour communicates to staff and students
partial_indicators: Uses technology effectively in communications and problem-solving but does not model it deliberately as a leadership practice or discuss their own technology use as an example for others

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders model the safe, ethical, and legal use of technology and the critical examination of digital content.
met_criteria: Publicly models critical engagement with digital content (e.g., evaluates a source, questions a claim)
Follows and discusses data ethics, copyright, and safety norms in their own practice
Raises ethical dimensions of institutional technology decisions in leadership conversations
Does not just state policies — models the practices they encode
not_yet_met_criteria: Delegates digital citizenship policy to pastoral or IT staff without personal modelling
Technology ethics are stated in policy but not embodied in leadership practice
partial_indicators: Ensures policy compliance with digital safety and legal requirements but does not model critical engagement with digital content or discuss the ethical dimensions of institutional technology decisions as a leader

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders include a wide range of perspectives from the community to develop and sustain a vision for using technology to advance student learning and success.
met_criteria: Engages a diverse stakeholder group including students, families, and community partners — not just staff
Uses structured processes to surface genuine community perspectives on technology and learning
The resulting vision reflects the community's aspirations, not just leadership priorities
Revisits the vision process periodically to include emerging perspectives
not_yet_met_criteria: Technology vision is developed by senior leaders without meaningful community engagement
Consultation is performative rather than generative
partial_indicators: Consults staff through surveys or focus groups but does not engage students, families, or community partners in the vision development process

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders build on the shared vision by collaboratively creating a strategic plan that articulates how technology will be used to enhance learning.
met_criteria: Strategic planning is a collaborative process — not a leadership task with staff sign-off
The plan explicitly maps technology investments to learning outcomes
Articulates how technology will change what and how students learn, not just what equipment they will have
The plan is owned and understood by those responsible for implementing it
not_yet_met_criteria: The strategic plan is produced by leadership with limited collaborative input
Technology strategy is framed around infrastructure and tools, not learning outcomes
partial_indicators: Involves staff in strategic planning through department head consultation but does not build a collaboratively owned plan or explicitly connect technology investments to student learning outcomes

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders evaluate progress on the strategic plan, make course corrections, measure impact and scale effective approaches for using technology to transform learning.
met_criteria: Has a structured evaluation process with defined metrics for assessing strategic plan progress
Makes documented course corrections based on evaluation findings
Distinguishes between scaling what works and persisting with what doesn't
Evaluation measures impact on learning, not just implementation activity
not_yet_met_criteria: Progress on the technology strategy is reported in terms of activities completed rather than outcomes achieved
Course corrections are not made systematically — the plan is followed even when evidence suggests it should change
partial_indicators: Reports progress against implementation milestones to governors and staff but does not measure impact on learning outcomes or systematically identify what should be scaled or changed

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders communicate effectively with stakeholders to gather input on the plan, celebrate successes and engage in a continuous improvement cycle.
met_criteria: Communication about the technology strategy is two-way — genuinely gathering input, not just reporting
Celebrates successes in ways that are meaningful to the community
Uses communication to maintain stakeholder engagement across the implementation cycle, not just at launch
Communication is part of a continuous improvement cycle, not a one-way channel
not_yet_met_criteria: Stakeholder communication about the technology strategy is primarily broadcast — updates and announcements, not dialogue
Input-gathering is limited to the strategy launch phase
partial_indicators: Communicates regularly about technology strategy progress and celebrates milestones publicly, but does not maintain channels for genuine ongoing input or connect communication explicitly to a continuous improvement cycle

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders share lessons learned, best practices, challenges and the impact of learning with technology with other education leaders who want to learn from this work.
met_criteria: Actively participates in inter-institutional networks where learning from technology strategy is shared
Shares challenges and failures as well as successes — not just best practice
Contributes to sector-wide knowledge about technology transformation in education
Positions their institution as a learning community within a broader system, not just a competitor
not_yet_met_criteria: Knowledge about technology strategy stays within the institution
Does not participate in external networks or contribute to sector learning
partial_indicators: Presents at a conference or network event about the school's technology work but does not maintain ongoing external engagement or share challenges and partial successes alongside achievements

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders empower educators to exercise professional agency, build teacher leadership skills and pursue personalized professional learning.
met_criteria: Creates structures where educators have genuine agency over their professional learning direction
Identifies and develops teacher leadership in technology, not just classroom practice
Personalized professional learning is resourced and supported, not just permitted
Educator agency is visible in how CPD is structured and evaluated
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional learning is centrally mandated with limited educator choice
Teacher leadership opportunities are informal and not systematically developed
Educators comply with professional learning requirements rather than pursuing them with ownership
partial_indicators: Offers a menu of CPD options and a professional learning fund but does not develop teacher leadership or support educators in designing genuinely personalized learning inquiries

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders build the confidence and competency of educators to put the ISTE Standards for Students and ISTE Standards for Educators into practice.
met_criteria: Professional development is explicitly framed around the ISTE Standards for Educators
Educators can identify which ISTE Standards they are developing and why
Confidence-building is addressed as a distinct dimension alongside competency
Progress in ISTE-aligned practice is recognisable and valued
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional development is not connected to the ISTE Standards framework
Educator competency development is measured in tool adoption, not pedagogical capability
partial_indicators: Provides professional development linked to technology tools and digital pedagogy, but the development is not explicitly framed around the ISTE Standards and educators do not develop the ability to self-assess against those standards

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders inspire a culture of innovation, creative problem-solving, and collaboration that allows the time to explore and develop teaching practices using digital tools.
met_criteria: Creates protected time for educators to experiment with technology in pedagogy
Celebrates and learns from experiments that did not produce the intended result
Innovation is a cultural value, not just a stated aspiration
Collaborative innovation is facilitated — educators develop practice together, not just individually
not_yet_met_criteria: Educators are expected to innovate without time, resource, or structural support
Risk-taking with technology is implicitly discouraged by accountability pressures
Innovation is celebrated only when it produces demonstrable results
partial_indicators: Celebrates innovative practice and encourages experimentation in communications, but does not create the protected time, structural support, or failure-positive culture needed for genuine pedagogical risk-taking with digital tools

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders support educators in using technology to advance learning that meets the diverse learning, cultural and social-emotional needs of individual students.
met_criteria: Has a clear understanding of the diverse needs present in their school population
Connects this understanding to technology investment and CPD decisions
Coaches educators on how technology can specifically serve diverse learner needs
Monitors whether technology use in classrooms is serving all students equitably
not_yet_met_criteria: Technology strategy does not account for the diverse learning, cultural, and social-emotional needs of students
Diversity is addressed in pastoral and inclusion policies but not in technology leadership decisions
partial_indicators: Ensures educators receive training on differentiation and inclusive practice but does not specifically connect this to technology decisions or monitor whether digital learning is serving diverse students equitably

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders develop learning assessments that provide a personalized, actionable view of student progress in real time.
met_criteria: Has invested in assessment infrastructure that provides personalised, real-time data
Educators use this data to adjust learning in near-real-time, not just at reporting intervals
Students have access to their own learning progress data in a form they can act on
Assessment systems support learning rather than just measuring it
not_yet_met_criteria: Assessment data is available only at reporting intervals
Data systems are designed for accountability rather than for learning improvement
Students do not have access to or agency over their learning progress data
partial_indicators: Has invested in a data dashboard that provides near-real-time class progress data for teachers but students do not have access to personalised views of their own progress and teachers primarily use data for reporting rather than real-time instructional adjustment

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders guide teams to establish equitable technology policies that support effective learning.
met_criteria: Technology policies are developed through a team process — not by leadership alone
Equity is an explicit criterion in policy development, not a downstream consideration
Policies are evaluated against student learning outcomes, not just compliance
Policy review is built into a regular governance cycle
not_yet_met_criteria: Technology policies are written by leadership or IT without equitable team process
Policies address safety and compliance but not equity or learning effectiveness
partial_indicators: Involves a steering group in policy development and ensures policies comply with legal equity requirements, but does not evaluate policies against learning outcomes or ensure equity beyond access provision

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders ensure that resources and infrastructure for supporting effective use of technology for learning are sufficient and scalable to meet future demand.
met_criteria: Infrastructure planning is connected to specific learning activity requirements, not just general capacity
Models future demand based on the learning programme, not just historical usage
Has a costed and phased replacement and upgrade plan
Scalability is an explicit design criterion, not just a hope
not_yet_met_criteria: Infrastructure investment is reactive — problems are addressed as they emerge
Infrastructure planning is disconnected from the learning programme and its technology requirements
partial_indicators: Has a device replacement cycle and adequate wifi capacity for current use but has not modelled future demand based on the learning programme or established scalability criteria for procurement decisions

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders protect privacy and security by ensuring staff understand and implement effective data management policies.
met_criteria: All staff understand their data management responsibilities, not just IT and admin
Data protection is embedded in onboarding, professional development, and tool procurement
Incident response processes are known and practised by the relevant staff
Privacy protection is a cultural value, not just a policy compliance requirement
not_yet_met_criteria: Data protection is delegated to IT and admin without general staff awareness or responsibility
Staff are told what the rules are but not equipped to apply them in varied contexts
partial_indicators: Ensures all staff complete data protection training and sign acceptable use policies, but this is compliance-focused training rather than building the practical understanding and habit of effective data management in daily professional practice

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders establish partnerships to advance strategic plans, achieve learning priorities and develop opportunities for students to gain real-world experience.
met_criteria: Partnerships are strategically chosen based on alignment with learning priorities
Student real-world experience is an explicit objective of at least one partnership
Partnerships are resourced and managed to deliver their intended learning benefits
Partnership value is reviewed against strategic plan goals, not just activity measures
not_yet_met_criteria: Partnerships are formed opportunistically rather than strategically
Student experience benefits from partnerships are incidental rather than designed
partial_indicators: Has established cost-sharing partnerships for technology procurement but does not leverage partnerships to advance learning priorities or create structured real-world experience opportunities for students

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders set goals to remain current on emerging technologies for learning, innovations in pedagogy and advancements in the learning sciences.
met_criteria: Has explicit personal learning goals related to technology and pedagogy
Reviews and updates these goals periodically
Current knowledge of emerging technologies and learning science informs strategic decisions
Can articulate recent shifts in their thinking about technology and learning
not_yet_met_criteria: Stays current through passive consumption (news feed, forwarded articles) without personal learning goals
Emerging technology awareness does not connect to strategic or pedagogical decisions
partial_indicators: Subscribes to edtech newsletters and reads regularly but has not set structured personal learning goals or used emerging knowledge to revise their strategic or pedagogical thinking

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders participate regularly in online professional learning networks to collaboratively learn with and mentor other professionals.
met_criteria: Is an active (contributing) member of at least one professional network focused on education leadership and technology
Mentors other professionals as well as learning from them
Network participation is regular — not just annual conference attendance
Network learning connects to institutional decisions and practice
not_yet_met_criteria: Professional networking is limited to in-person events or passive online presence
Does not mentor peers or contribute to collective learning in their field
partial_indicators: Attends professional networks and conferences regularly and maintains LinkedIn connections but does not actively contribute, mentor others, or bring network learning systematically back into institutional decision-making

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders use technology to regularly engage in reflective practices that support personal and professional growth.
met_criteria: Has a structured reflective practice that uses technology (e.g., leadership journal, reflective recording, annotated reading)
Reflection is regular, not just at crisis points
Technological reflection supports genuine growth — it changes thinking or practice
Models reflective practice to staff as a professional norm
not_yet_met_criteria: Does not have a structured reflective practice
Reflection happens in response to problems rather than as a regular developmental habit
partial_indicators: Keeps a leadership journal and reflects on significant decisions but does not use technology to structure or enhance reflection, and reflection is not modelled to staff as a professional norm

indicators.indicator_source_text: Leaders develop the skills needed to lead and navigate change, advance systems and promote a mindset of continuous improvement for how technology can improve learning.
met_criteria: Has a developed repertoire of change leadership strategies, not just willingness to change
Understands system interdependencies and how technology change ripples across the organisation
Actively promotes a continuous improvement mindset — including willingness to revise the strategy
Develops change leadership capacity in others, not just exercises it themselves
not_yet_met_criteria: Approaches change primarily as an implementation challenge — plans, communicates, monitors
Does not account for system interdependencies or develop change leadership capacity in others
Continuous improvement is a stated value but not a practised process
partial_indicators: Manages technology change effectively in terms of planning and stakeholder communication but does not develop the adaptive, system-navigation, or capacity-building dimensions of change leadership that this standard requires
